name: LED1642GWTTR
title: LED1642GW: 16-channel constant-current LED sink driver with 12/16-bit PWM, gain control and LED fault detection
summary: Sixteen regulated current sinks rated to 20 V, fed by a 30 MHz serial shift-register interface (SDI, CLK, LE, SDO) for LED displays and signage. One resistor sets the reference current; a 7-bit gain code (six bits plus a range bit) trims it from about 3 mA to 36 mA, and each channel has its own 12- or 16-bit PWM brightness clocked from PWCLK. It detects open and shorted LEDs, flags temperature above 150 °C and shuts down at 170 °C, offers selectable edge times, staggered turn-on, an auto power-down and a falling-edge SDO option for chains. Supply is 3 V to 5.5 V.

circuits.title: Typical application schematic
circuits.description: Sixteen LEDs hang from one common LED rail, each cathode on its own OUTn sink, so every LED carries the channel current the chip regulates. CLED holds up the LED rail and CIN decouples VDD. REXT from R-EXT to ground sets the reference current for all channels. SDI, CLK and LE carry serial data and commands from a controller, PWCLK takes the clock that drives the brightness counter, and SDO passes data on to the next device or back to the controller.

operation.text: Each of the 16 sinks delivers 3 mA to 40 mA. The regulated range across settings is 0.5 mA to 36 mA, with accuracy figures holding only in the conditions of the electrical table.

Data enters SDI on each CLK rising edge into a 16-bit shift register. LE both latches data and chooses its destination: the count of CLK rising edges seen while LE is high forms a digital key that selects the switch register, brightness latches, configuration register, error detection or the thermal flag read. CLK runs to 30 MHz in a cascade. SDO carries the shifted data on to the next device in a daisy chain.
A 16-bit word ending with the write-switch key (1 or 2 CLK edges with LE high) turns channels on or off, bit 0F sent first and bit 00 last.

A 16-bit word ending with key 7 writes the register; key 8 reads it back on SDO over the next 16 clocks. Every bit is 0 at power-up or after reset, which means low current range at gain 0, normal error detection, short threshold 1.8 V, auto OFF disabled, fastest edges, no SDO delay, gradual delay on and a 16-bit PWM counter.

REXT to GND and the CFG-6 range bit fix the current at power-up; the six gain bits then add up to 63 steps, each one twenty-first of that starting current. With 11 kΩ the low range spans 3.131 mA to 12.524 mA and the high range 8.945 mA to 35.78 mA. REXT may be up to 100 kΩ.

Keep REXT right at the R-EXT and GND pins with short traces so that noise and interference do not reach the reference. Returning it to the chip's own GND pin also limits shifts in output current when total ground current changes.

Each channel has its own brightness register compared against a counter clocked from PWCLK; CFG-15 picks a 16-bit counter (65536 steps) or a 12-bit one (4096 steps, the top four bits of each word ignored, though every word is still 16 bits long). Words go in MSB first, channel 15 first and channel 0 last: each of the first fifteen ends with the data-latch key (3–4 edges) and the last with the global-latch key (5–6 edges), which moves all 16 buffers into the brightness registers together. Registers start at 0, the minimum brightness. PWCLK is a square wave of any duty cycle with pulses at least 20 ns wide and a frequency up to 30 MHz. Right after start-up, before PWCLK runs, any channel with a non-zero brightness value is on.

With CFG-7 = 0, a channel is tested by switching it on in the switch register with non-zero brightness, sending the open (9 edges), short (10) or combined (11) start key, keeping the output on for at least 1 µs, then sending the end key (12). The last on-time inside the window must begin at least 0.5 µs before the end key. Because PWCLK is often not synchronous with CLK, the test is best run just after start-up with all channels on and before PWCLK is applied. The result comes out of SDO over the next 16 clocks, channel 15 first, with 0 marking a fault. With the SDO delay off, channel 15's bit is valid after the first rising edge and is sampled on the second; channel 0's is sampled on the 17th.

The open test flags a channel whose current stays at or below half the programmed value (open LED or output shorted to ground). The short test flags a channel whose output voltage is above the CFG-9/CFG-8 threshold of 1.8 V, 2.5 V, 3.0 V or 3.5 V (LED shorted, or output shorted to the LED rail). Combined mode checks both.

With CFG-10 = 1 the chip powers down its internals once latched data turns every channel off, drawing 200 µA typ, and wakes when a latched word turns any channel on again (shutdown about 100 ns, wake about 3 µs after LE falls). While shut down it responds only to the command that turns channels on.
CFG-12 and CFG-11 select the current rise and fall time (20 % to 80 %) from four pairs: 30/20 ns, 100/40 ns, 140/80 ns and 180/150 ns.

By default SDO changes on the CLK rising edge, about 15 ns later. With CFG-13 = 1 it changes on the CLK falling edge instead, a few ns after it, which helps daisy chains where board routing skews CLK against the SDO data.

With CFG-14 = 0, outputs switched on together by the PWM counter start one after another, 10 ns apart, about 150 ns from first to last. This limits inrush current and lets the bypass capacitor be smaller. CFG-14 = 1 turns all outputs on at once.

Above 150 °C an internal flag is set; above 170 °C the outputs shut down. Holding LE high for 13 CLK rising edges loads the flag, and the next 16 clocks shift it out of SDO as sixteen 1s when hot or sixteen 0s when not.
Each output needs a minimum voltage across it to regulate its current; below that voltage the current is lower than the setting, and any voltage above it raises the power dissipated in the chip.
The chip starts above a rising threshold of 2.7 V typ (2.9 V max) and stops below 2.3 V typ, with 400 mV hysteresis.
LE has an internal pull-down and PWCLK an internal pull-up, both 500 kΩ typ. CLK and SDI have none and must be held at a defined level by the circuit driving them.
QFN-24 and TSSOP24 exposed pad reach their low thermal resistance only with the pad soldered to the board, either to an isolated copper land or to ground.
